* 1. initGraph
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: editor/initGraph
:FILE: resources/packages/app/editor/editor-main.js
:LINE: 222
:MINS: 5.5

 *Start here for anything you can click.* The editor is ~75 plain ~.js~ files concatenated into one bundle in a fixed order (no imports, no build step — the per-module map is in [[../EDITOR_MODULES.md][docs/EDITOR_MODULES.md]]), and this is the boot. Note the shape of the fetches: the namespace TREE goes out alone first, because its status answers the auth question for everyone — only a non-401 fires the three secondary loads. Fn leaves and per-fn slots/bindings arrive lazily; a 401 sends the user to sign in rather than into a red fatal banner.

The client mirror of the compile layer's ~build-lookups~: the same raw fn / slot / fn-slot / binding / list-item rows, indexed into the O(1) Maps every render path reads (~fnMap~, ~slotByFnAndName~, ~bindingByFnSlot~, ~itemsByBinding~, the namespace-path map). The graph itself: two Maps plus two adjacency indexes and an ~animating~ flag. This is *all* that remained of cytoscape when it was removed — the library had been reduced to a node/edge store and a position tween, so it became this file. ~window.graphView~ is the surface Playwright tests wait on (~ready()~, ~animating()~), which is why the browser-test suite never needed rewriting.

* 4. fetchBackendLayout
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: editor/fetchBackendLayout
:FILE: resources/packages/app/editor/editor-layout.js
:LINE: 278
:MINS: 10.9
:END:

The client does NOT lay the graph out. It POSTs the selected root plus the per-node expansion spec to ~/api/graph/layout~ and gets back nodes, edges and a ~nodeId → {x, y, row, col}~ map. This is the wire crossing into the previous block: the server owns grid topology, the client owns pixels.

Most of its length is the sizing pass that runs AFTER the response: per-column widths, then per-column gaps computed from the widest edge label plus the type chips and badges the overlays render beside it. That is the client's one real layout responsibility — making the server's grid fit the pixels its own cards actually occupy. Read the POST at the top, then jump to the comment blocks that explain each gap term.

* 5. renderGraph
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: editor/renderGraph
:FILE: resources/packages/app/editor/editor-render.js
:LINE: 98
:MINS: 9.1
:END:

One render cycle, and the reason it is not a one-liner: prime the selected fn's subtree, capture an ANCHOR node before the await so the canvas doesn't jump under the cursor, fetch the layout, diff it against the live graph, then re-measure — card heights are only known after the overlays exist, so the server's grid is corrected against measured DOM and the nodes settle onto the result.

A node is not drawn — it is an absolutely-positioned HTML card riding the layer transform (edges are SVG; everything else is DOM). :FILE: resources/packages/web/runtime/graphden-runtime.js

The pivot from client logic to server-rendered HTML. ONE delegated listener per host resolves ~data-action="…"~ against a registry filled by ~registerActionHandler~, so a fragment the server just rendered becomes interactive with no per-fragment wiring. This file is platform-shared: it is bundled into the editor AND served standalone at ~/assets/graphden-runtime.js~, so user-composed pages get the same dispatch. Read the bind-once comment — without it a reused singleton popover fires ~delete-fn~ N times on the Nth open.

Fetch an HTML partial, swap it into a host, re-bind the dispatcher. That is the whole ~/partials/*~ client contract ([[../PARTIALS.md][docs/PARTIALS.md]]) — the migration path by which popovers that used to be hand-built DOM became graph-native fn-defs. The supersession token is the subtle part: two concurrent loads into one host must let the LATEST call win, not the fastest response.

How an edit actually happens. The control is not chosen here: the client POSTs the slot to ~/api/value-form~ and the graph's value-form registry answers with hiccup naming a widget — the editor routes on ~data-form-widget~ and knows no type tags at all. Note ~onSaved~: a value change alters binding rows, so ~lookups~ is stale and the handler re-fetches rather than re-rendering.

* 11. gdEnterDiffMode
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: editor/gdEnterDiffMode
:FILE: resources/packages/app/editor/editor-diff-mode.js
:LINE: 1283
:MINS: 3.6
:END:

COMPARE MODE — THE diff surface, entered by picking the second branch (the Δ on a popover row; click again to exit). One fetch of the grouped ~diff-view~ payload, then pure annotation: Explorer rows badge +/±/−, namespace headers aggregate counts, a LENS BAR under the kind chips filters the tree by change type (~gdDiffSetLens~ — only-changed, kind toggles, substantive-only, effects-touched-only), changed fn cards and args ring on the canvas (~gdDiffModeCardInfo~ / ~gdDiffSlotsForFn~), a selected changed fn gets an inspector DIFF PANEL (~gdDiffRenderInspectorSection~ — old → new entries, effects delta, anchored 💬 threads), and the Δ chip persists the mode across reloads. The chip's menu is the review cockpit: Review & comments dialog, propose-current-for-review, merge-compared-in. Fns existing only on the compared branch inject as ghost rows; effect-set deltas come from a FULL per-branch registry comparison (~gdDiffEffectSetDelta~ — the registry is branch-scoped), with the changed-refs signal (~gdDiffEffectsTouched~) as the anonymous-fn fallback. Note what it does NOT do: no data re-routing — every read and write stays on the current branch, so the user keeps editing with the lens on.

- source :: [[file:../../../resources/packages/app/editor/editor-diff-mode.js::async function gdEnterDiffMode(otherBranch) {][resources/packages/app/editor/editor-diff-mode.js:1283]]

* 12. gdApplyThemePayload
:PROPERTIES:

:FILE: resources/packages/app/editor/editor-prefs.js
:LINE: 361
:MINS: 1.9

A THEME (Settings → Appearance, docs/MARKETPLACE.md § 5) is a payload ~{mode tokens fonts scale}~ applied as INLINE custom properties on ~<body>~ — inline beats ~body.theme-dark {…}~, so it wins in either base and clears cleanly. Read ~sanitizeThemePayload~ just above: a shared theme is another user's data, so only allow-listed tokens with colour literals get through; a ~url()~ or a second declaration is dropped. The mirror in localStorage is applied before first paint; the server preference reconciles after boot.

* 13. gdApplyKeymap
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: editor/gdApplyKeymap
:FILE: resources/packages/app/editor/editor-shortcuts.js
:LINE: 81
:MINS: 1.3
:END:

A keyboard LAYOUT is an overrides map ~{id {keys leader}}~ over the shortcut registry. ~_defaults~ remembers each id's declared keys the first time it registers (reset is possible), and ~registerShortcut~ consults ~_overrides~ on every registration — so the canvas's late ~g g~ still lands on the user's keys. Settings → Keyboard renders ~gdShortcutEntries()~; the which-key menu and the ~?~ cheatsheet show the rebound keys because they already read the registry.

* 14. authFetch
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: editor/authFetch
:FILE: resources/packages/app/editor/editor-auth.js
:LINE: 144
:MINS: 1.4
:END:

Every mutating call in the editor goes through this. It is 12 lines and worth all of them: a 401 clears the stored credential and re-opens the sign-in popover in place. The trap to internalize before you write editor code — ~authFetch~ and ~authMutate~ *resolve* on 4xx, they do not throw. A caller that only wraps them in ~try/catch~ counts a rejected write as a success.

* 15. _tourTick
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: editor/_tourTick
:FILE: resources/packages/app/editor/editor-tour.js
:LINE: 677
:MINS: 3.9
:END:

Closing the loop back to the user tutorial: the in-editor guided lessons are graph content (~app.tour/_tour-lessons~, served at ~GET /api/tour~) and this file is only the engine that interprets them. Each tick clears the reader-state traps that make a lesson unfinishable — a collapsed Explorer, a kind lens hiding the very fn the step names, a target scrolled out of view — then polls the step's declarative check and advances. A tour that can dead-end is worse than no tour, which is what every guard here is paying for.
